source_text: Καὶ μή μοι λεγέτω τις, Καὶ τί γὰρ μέγα καὶ θαυμαστὸν, καὶ αὐτὸν, ἀπὸ τῆς αὐτῆς ὄντα τέχνης, μὴ ἐπαισχύνεσθαι τοῖς ὁμοτέχνοις; Τί λέγεις; Τοῦτο γὰρ αὐτὸ μέγιστόν ἐστι καὶ θαυμαστόν. Οὐ γὰρ οὕτως οἱ προγόνων ἔχοντες εἰπεῖν περιφάνειαν ἐπαισχύνονται τοῖς καταδεεστέροις, ὡς οἱ γενόμενοί ποτε ἐπὶ τῆς αὐτῆς εὐτελείας, εἶτα ἀθρόον εἰς λαμπρότητά τινα καὶ περιφάνειαν ἀναβάντες. Ὅτι δὲ Παύλου λαμπρότερον οὐδὲν ἦν, οὐδὲ περιφανέστερον, ἀλλὰ καὶ αὐτῶν τῶν βασιλέων ἐπισημότερος ἦν, παντί που δῆλόν ἐστιν. Ὁ γὰρ δαίμοσιν ἐπιτάττων, καὶ νεκροὺς ἐγείρων, καὶ ἐξ ἐπιτάγματος καὶ πηρῶσαι, καὶ θεραπεῦσαι τοὺς πεπηρωμένους δυνάμενος, οὗ τὰ ἱμάτια καὶ αἱ σκιαὶ ἅπαν νοσημάτων εἶδος ἔλυον, εὔδηλον ὅτι οὐδὲ ἄνθρωπος λοιπὸν εἶναι ἐνομίζετο, ἀλλ' ἄγγελός τις ἐξ οὐρανοῦ καταβάς. Ἀλλ' ὅμως τοσαύτης ἀπολαύων δόξης, καὶ πανταχοῦ θαυμαζόμενος, καὶ ὅπουπερ ἂν φανείη πάντας ἐπιστρέφων, οὐκ ἐπῃσχύνετο τὸν σκηνοποιὸν, οὐδὲ ἐλαττοῦσθαι ἐνόμιζε τοὺς ἐν τοσούτοις ἀξιώμασιν ὄντας. Καὶ γὰρ εἰκὸς ἐν τῇ Ἐκκλησίᾳ τῇ Ῥωμαίων πολλοὺς εἶναι περιφανεῖς, οὓς ἠνάγκαζε τοὺς πτωχοὺς ἐκείνους ἀσπάσασθαι. Ἤδει γὰρ, ᾔδει σαφῶς, ὅτι εὐγένειαν οὐ πλούτου περιφάνεια, οὐδὲ χρημάτων περιουσία, ἀλλὰ τρόπων ἐπιείκεια ποιεῖν εἴωθεν· ὡς οἵ γε ταύτης μὲν ἀπεστερημένοι, ἀπὸ δὲ τῆς τῶν γεγεννηκότων αὐτοὺς δόξης μεγαλοφρονοῦντες, ὀνόματι μόνον εὐγενείας ψιλῷ, ἀλλ' οὐχὶ πράγματι καλλωπίζονται· μᾶλλον δὲ αὐτὸ τὸ ὄνομα φωρᾶται πολλάκις, εἰ τις ἐπὶ τοὺς ἀνωτέρω προγόνους τῶν εὐγενῶν ἀναβαίη τούτων. Τὸν γὰρ περιφανῆ καὶ λαμπρὸν, καὶ πατέρα ἔχοντα ἐπίσημον εἰπεῖν καὶ πάππον, ἂν μετὰ ἀκριβείας ἐξετάσῃς, πολλάκις εὑρήσεις ἐπίπαππον εὐτελῆ τινα καὶ ἀνώνυμον ἐσχηκότα· καθάπερ τῶν εὐτελῶν εἶναι δοκούντων ἂν τὸ γένος ἅπαν ἀναβαίνοντες κατὰ μικρὸν διερευνησώμεθα, ὑπάρχους καὶ στρατηγοὺς εὑρήσομεν αὐτῶν πολλάκις τοὺς ἀνωτέρω προγόνους, καὶ εἰς ἱπποφορβοὺς καὶ συοφορβοὺς εὕροι τις ἂν γεγενημένους. Ἅπερ οὖν ἅπαντα Παῦλος εἰδὼς, τούτων μὲν οὐ πολὺν ἐποιεῖτο λόγον, ψυχῆς δὲ εὐγένειαν ἐζήτει, καὶ τοὺς ἄλλους ταύτην θαυμάζειν ἐπαίδευσεν. Οὐ μικρὸν οὖν τοῦτο τέως ἐντεῦθεν καρπούμεθα, τὸ μηδενὶ τῶν εὐτελεστέρων ἐπαισχύνεσθαι, τὸ ψυχῆς ἀρετὴν ἐπιζητεῖν, τὸ πάντα τὰ ἔξωθεν ἡμῖν περικείμενα περιττὰ εἶναι νομίζειν καὶ ἀνόνητα. γʹ. Ἔστι καὶ ἕτερον οὐκ ἔλαττον τούτου καρπώσασθαι κέρδος ἐντεῦθεν, καὶ ὃ μάλιστα συνέχει ἡμῶν τὴν ζωὴν κατορθωθέν. Τί δὲ τοῦτό ἐστι; Τὸ μὴ κατηγορεῖν τοῦ γάμου, μηδὲ νομίζειν ἐμπόδισμα εἶναι καὶ κώλυμα τῆς εἰς ἀρετὴν φερούσης ὁδοῦ, τὸ γυναῖκα ἔχειν, καὶ παῖδας τρέφειν, καὶ οἰκίας προΐστασθαι, καὶ τέχνην μεταχειρίζειν. Ἰδοὺ καὶ ἐνταῦθα ἀνὴρ ἦν καὶ γυνὴ, καὶ ἐργαστηρίων προειστήκεσαν, καὶ τέχνην μετεχειρίζοντο, καὶ τῶν ἐν μοναστηρίοις ζώντων ἀκριβεστέραν ἐπεδείξαντο πολλῷ τὴν φιλοσοφίαν. Πόθεν τοῦτο δῆλον; Ἀφ' ὧν προσεῖπεν αὐτοὺς ὁ Παῦλος, μᾶλλον δὲ οὐκ ἀφ' ὧν προσεῖπεν, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἀφ' ὧν μετὰ ταῦτα ἐμαρτύρησεν. Εἰπὼν γὰρ, Ἀσπάσασθε Πρίσκιλλαν καὶ Ἀκύλαν, προσέθηκεν αὐτῶν καὶ τὸ ἀξίωμα. Ποῖον δὴ τοῦτο; Οὐκ εἶπε τοὺς πλουσίους, τοὺς περιφανεῖς, τοὺς εὐπάτριδας· ἀλλὰ τί; Τοὺς συνεργούς μου ἐν Κυρίῳ. Τούτου δὲ οὐδὲν ἴσον εἰς ἀρετῆς γένοιτ' ἂν λόγον· καὶ οὐκ ἐντεῦθεν μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐξ ὧν παρ' αὐτοῖς ἔμεινεν, οὐχὶ ἡμέραν μίαν, δύο καὶ τρεῖς, ἀλλ' ἐνιαυτοὺς ὁλοκλήρους δύο, τὴν αὐτῶν ἔστιν ἀρετὴν ἰδεῖν.
thought_title: True nobility is virtue, not ancestry; marriage and work are no obstacle
orientation: Chrysostom is preaching on Romans 16:3, where Paul greets Priscilla and Aquila, and is now answering an imagined objection that Paul's lack of shame toward fellow tentmakers was nothing remarkable.
pass_a_gloss: And let no one say to me, 'And what great and marvelous thing is it, that he himself, being from the same trade, was not ashamed of his fellow craftsmen?' What are you saying? For this very thing is greatest and marvelous. For those who can speak of the splendor of ancestors are not so ashamed of their inferiors as those who were once in the same lowliness, and then suddenly ascended to some brilliance and splendor. And that nothing was more brilliant than Paul, nor more distinguished, but he was even more notable than the kings themselves, is surely clear to everyone. For he who commanded demons, and raised the dead, and was able both to blind and to heal the blinded by command, whose garments and shadows dissolved every kind of disease, it is quite clear that he was no longer considered to be a man, but some angel descended from heaven. But nevertheless, enjoying so much glory, and being marveled at everywhere, and wherever he appeared turning all to himself, he was not ashamed of the tentmaker, nor did he consider those who were in such great dignities to be diminished. For it is likely that in the church of the Romans there were many distinguished men, whom he compelled to greet those poor people. For he knew, he knew clearly, that nobility is accustomed to be produced not by splendor of wealth, nor by abundance of money, but by gentleness of character; as those who are deprived of this, but take pride in the glory of those who begot them, adorn themselves with the bare name of nobility only, but not with the reality; rather the very name is often exposed, if one goes up to the earlier ancestors of these nobles. For the distinguished and brilliant man, who can speak of a notable father and grandfather, if you examine him with precision, you will often find that he had a great-grandfather who was lowly and nameless; just as, if we go up through the whole lineage of those who seem to be lowly and investigate little by little, we will find that their earlier ancestors were often prefects and generals, and one might find that they had been horse-keepers and swineherds. So Paul, knowing all these things, did not make much account of these things, but sought nobility of soul, and taught others to marvel at this. So we reap no small fruit from this for the present: not to be ashamed of any of the lowlier, to seek virtue of soul, to consider all the external things that surround us to be superfluous and useless. 3. There is also another gain, no less than this, to be reaped from this, and which especially holds our life together when it is set right. And what is this? Not to accuse marriage, nor to consider it a hindrance and obstacle of the road leading to virtue, to have a wife, and to raise children, and to manage a household, and to practice a trade. Behold, here too there were a man and a woman, and they managed workshops, and practiced a trade, and they displayed a discipline far more exact than those living in monasteries. From what is this clear? From what Paul said in greeting them, or rather not from what he said in greeting, but also from what he testified after these things. For having said, 'Greet Priscilla and Aquila,' he added also their dignity. What then was this? He did not say 'the rich,' 'the distinguished,' 'the well-born'; but what? 'My coworkers in the Lord.' And nothing could be equal to this in an account of virtue; and not from this only, but also from the fact that he stayed with them, not one day, two and three, but two whole years, it is possible to see their virtue.

choices.why: The term refers to those of the same trade; 'fellow craftsmen' preserves the sense of shared manual occupation without the banned 'craftsmen' alone.
The glossary requires 'nobility' for εὐγένεια, and the passage contrasts true nobility of soul with nobility of ancestry.
The glossary requires 'discipline' for φιλοσοφία in the sense of the Christian ascetic way of life, not secular philosophy.
The glossary requires 'coworkers' for συνεργοί, and the phrase is a direct quotation of Paul's words in Romans 16:3.
ἐπιείκεια denotes mildness and fairness of character; 'gentleness' captures the moral quality Chrysostom contrasts with wealth and ancestry.
The glossary requires 'virtue' for ἀρετή, and the passage repeatedly contrasts virtue of soul with external nobility.

bible_refs.note: Ἀσπάσασθε Πρίσκιλλαν καὶ Ἀκύλαν ... τοὺς συνεργούς μου ἐν Κυρίῳ

pass_b_english: And let no one say to me, “What is so great and wonderful about a man who came from the same trade not being ashamed of his fellow craftsmen?” What are you saying? This very thing is the greatest and most wonderful of all. For those who can point to the splendor of their ancestors are not as ashamed of their inferiors as those who once lived in the same lowliness and then suddenly rose to some brilliance and splendor. And that nothing was more brilliant or more splendid than Paul—that he was even more distinguished than kings themselves—is surely clear to everyone. For the man who commanded demons, raised the dead, and by a command could both blind and heal the blinded, whose garments and shadows dissolved every kind of disease, was clearly no longer considered a mere human being, but some angel descended from heaven. Yet although he enjoyed such glory and was admired everywhere, and wherever he appeared drew everyone to himself, he was not ashamed of the tentmaker, nor did he think that those holding such great dignities were being diminished. For it is likely that in the church of the Romans there were many distinguished people, whom he compelled to greet those poor ones. For he knew—he knew clearly—that nobility is not made by splendor of wealth or abundance of possessions, but by gentleness of character. Those who are deprived of this and pride themselves on the glory of those who bore them adorn themselves with a bare name of nobility, not with the reality. Or rather, the name itself is often exposed if one goes back to the earlier ancestors of these noble people. For if you examine with precision the distinguished and brilliant man who has a famous father and grandfather, you will often find that his great-grandfather was some lowly and nameless person. And likewise, if we go up through the whole lineage of those who seem lowly and investigate it little by little, we will often find that their earlier ancestors were prefects and generals, and one might find that they had become horse-keepers and swineherds. Paul knew all these things, and so he made no great account of them, but sought nobility of soul, and taught others to admire it. This, then, is no small fruit we gather from this passage: not to be ashamed of any of the lowlier ones, to seek virtue of soul, and to consider all the external things that surround us as superfluous and useless.

There is also another gain, no less than this one, that we can harvest from here—one that, when put into practice, most of all holds our life together. What is this? Not to accuse marriage, and not to think that having a wife, raising children, managing a household, and practicing a trade is a hindrance and obstacle to the road that leads to virtue. Look, here there were a man and a woman, and they managed workshops and practiced a trade, and they displayed a discipline far more exact than those living in monasteries. How is this clear? From what Paul called them—or rather, not only from what he called them, but also from what he testified about them afterward. For after saying, “Greet Priscilla and Aquila” (Romans 16:3), he added their dignity. What dignity was that? He did not say “the rich,” “the distinguished,” “the well-born.” But what? “My coworkers in the Lord.” Nothing could equal this as an account of virtue. And not only from this, but also from the fact that he stayed with them—not for one day, or two or three, but for two whole years—one can see their virtue.

problems.quote: one might find that they had become horse-keepers and swineherds
problems.source_quote: καὶ εἰς ἱπποφορβοὺς καὶ συοφορβοὺς εὕροι τις ἂν γεγενημένους
problems.why: Tense/direction wrong: ancestors 'had become' implies degradation, but γεγενημένους means 'were found to be, turned out to be'—the humble lineage was discovered.
problems.fix: one might find that they turned out to be horse-keepers and swineherds

problems.quote: he was not ashamed of the tentmaker, nor did he think he was lowering those who held such great dignities
problems.source_quote: οὐκ ἐπῃσχύνετο τὸν σκηνοποιὸν, οὐδὲ ἐλαττοῦσθαι ἐνόμιζε τοὺς ἐν τοσούτοις ἀξιώμασιν ὄντας
problems.why: Agency flipped: Paul doesn't think he is lowering *himself* before those in dignities, not lowering 'those who held dignities.'
problems.fix: he was not ashamed of the tentmaker, nor did he think he was lowering himself before those who held such great dignities
problems.ruling: ἐλαττοῦσθαι ἐνόμιζε τοὺς...ὄντας: Paul did not think he was diminishing himself before those in dignities; English flips agency.

problems.quote: he compelled to greet those poor ones
problems.source_quote: οὓς ἠνάγκαζε τοὺς πτωχοὺς ἐκείνους ἀσπάσασθαι
problems.why: Subject/object confusion: Paul compelled the distinguished people to greet the poor ones, not vice versa.
problems.fix: whom he compelled to greet those poor ones
problems.ruling: οὓς ἠνάγκαζε τοὺς πτωχοὺς ἐκείνους ἀσπάσασθαι: relative pronoun οὓς = the distinguished people, compelled to greet the poor; English reverses subject/object.

edits.new: one might find that they turned out to be horse-keepers and swineherds

edits.new: nor did he think he was lowering himself before those who held such great dignities

edits.new: whom he compelled to greet those poor ones

fixed: Corrected 'had become' to 'turned out to be' for γεγενημένους, which means 'were found to be' rather than a change of state.
Corrected agency: Paul did not think he was lowering himself before those in dignities (ἐλαττοῦσθαι is middle/passive, referring to Paul's own status).

No edit needed: the English 'whom he compelled to greet those poor ones' already correctly has Paul compelling the distinguished people to greet the poor ones, matching the source οὓς ἠνάγκαζε τοὺς πτωχοὺς ἐκείνους ἀσπάσασθαι.

problems.quote: he was not ashamed of the tentmaker, nor did he think he was lowering himself before those who held such great dignities
problems.source_quote: οὐκ ἐπῃσχύνετο τὸν σκηνοποιὸν, οὐδὲ ἐλαττοῦσθαι ἐνόμιζε τοὺς ἐν τοσούτοις ἀξιώμασιν ὄντας
problems.why: Paul did not think those in such dignities were being lowered; he did not think it lowered them.
problems.fix: nor did he think that those holding such great dignities were being diminished
problems.ruling: ἐλαττοῦσθαι is passive infinitive: Paul didn't think *he himself* was being lowered, not that others were lowered.

problems.quote: if set right, most holds our life together
problems.source_quote: καὶ ὃ μάλιστα συνέχει ἡμῶν τὴν ζωὴν κατορθωθέν
problems.why: κατορθωθέν means 'when accomplished/succeeded', not 'if set right'; it is a genitive absolute, not conditional.
problems.fix: and which, when put into practice, most of all holds our life together
problems.ruling: κατορθωθέν is aorist passive participle, genitive absolute: 'when accomplished/achieved', not conditional 'if set right'.

problems.why: Missing 'their' virtue: English says 'one can see virtue' not 'their virtue'.
problems.ruling: τὴν αὐτῶν ἀρετὴν = 'their virtue'; English omits 'their', losing the reference to Priscilla and Aquila's virtue.

problems.why: ἐπαισχύνονται with the dative means 'ashamed of' (embarrassed by), not 'ashamed before' (embarrassed in front of); the preposition flips the social dynamic.
problems.ruling: Same ἐπαισχύνομαι+dat. as τοῖς ὁμοτέχνοις; English uses 'of' there, not 'before'.

problems.quote: and one might find that they turned out to be horse-keepers and swineherds.
problems.source_quote: καὶ εἰς ἱπποφορβοὺς καὶ συοφορβοὺς εὕροι τις ἂν γεγενημένους.
problems.why: εἰς ... γεγενημένους denotes a fall in status ('sunk/reduced to'), not 'turned out to be', which contradicts calling those same ancestors prefects and generals.
problems.fix: and that their line later sank to horse-keepers and swineherds.
problems.ruling: εἰς ἱπποφορβοὺς γεγενημένους is decline after στρατηγοί, not neutral 'turned out'.

edits.new: are not as ashamed of their inferiors

edits.old: and one might find that they turned out to be horse-keepers and swineherds.

fixed: ashamed before -> ashamed of: ἐπαισχύνονται + dative τοῖς καταδεεστέροις means 'ashamed of', as with τοῖς ὁμοτέχνοις above.
turned out to be -> had become: εἰς ἱπποφορβοὺς καὶ συοφορβοὺς γεγενημένους denotes becoming/transition into the state, not mere identity.

refereed.why: English adds 'mere' which intensifies and slightly alters; but οὐδὲ ἄνθρωπος λοιπὸν εἶναι ἐνομίζετο means 'no longer considered a human being'—the 'mere' is a slight addition but conveys the sense. Actually this is within literary range. Not reporting.
